subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REGULATIONS RESPECTING ORDERLY PAYMENT OF DEBTS

speakeroldname: Hon. Ron Basford (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REGULATIONS RESPECTING ORDERLY PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce today amendments in regulations under the Bankruptcy Act to expand the scope of procedures under Part X of the Act, which provides for debt consolidation and orderly repayment by individual wage earners.
The regulations under Part X of the Act have been proclaimed and are in force in the provinces which have chosen to implement it-Nova Scotia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta. Consultation is under way with two other provinces wishing to take advantage of the federal legislation, British Columbia and Prince Edward Island.
The changes in the regulations being approved today remove any limit on the amount of debt which a province may allow wage earners to consolidate through a court order. Until now the limit has been $1,000. Manitoba has already chosen to double the limit to $2,000, and Saskatchewan and Alberta have decided to let the procedure apply to debts of any amount.
A brief word on the nature of the plan might be helpful to hon. members. In the provinces where the Act is in force, individuals may apply to a court clerk for an order consolidating their debts and setting out the terms and schedule of repayment, and the court approves a plan within the debtor's means. The regular payments are distributed among the creditors on a pro rata basis until the debts are fully repaid. Until the debts are entirely repaid, the individual is immune from legal proceedings and cannot be sued by his creditors. At the same time, the individual is prohibited from contracting new debts.
This plan can provide badly needed assistance to unfortunate wage earners who cannot cope with their debts and who cannot afford the more costly step of declaring a personal bankruptcy. From the creditor's point of view, it means he can give the debtor time to pay without any fear that another creditor might seize the assets of the debtor through legal proceedings.
I wish to emphasize that the entire Bankruptcy Act is being reviewed with a view to complete revision, including Part X, but I consider the relief these changes make right away to be so desirable that I wanted to go as far as we can now with the existing act. However, some provincial Attorneys General may quite properly wish to wait until a complete revision of the Act is dealt with by Parliament before requesting that the existing Part X be declared in force in their province.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Parliament has been waiting a long time now for a ministerial announcement in connection with revision of the Bankruptcy Act. When the minister rose in his place today I was hopeful that at long last the statement he was about to make might be a

May 7, 1970
Bankruptcy Act
preliminary announcement of that event. Instead, today he has made an announcement dealing with debt consolidation and the orderly repayment of debts on the part of individual wage earners. I understand the importance of this matter and I am aware that it was discussed in committee by the hon. member for St. John's East as recently as last week.
As the minister emphasized, there is some urgency in dealing with this matter prior to the comprehensive revision of the Bankruptcy Act because Canadians are falling deeper and deeper in debt as a result of the dual pressures of the rising cost of living under runaway inflation and the growing unemployment. This is true in all parts of Canada and in all sectors of the economy.
As the minister has indicated, I believe it is significant that the provinces which have already acted on this problem are located mainly in western Canada. Manitoba has raised the limit of debt consolidation from $1,000 to $2,000 and Saskatchewan and Alberta are applying the procedure without limit; in other words, there is no ceiling restriction. This is understandable when one considers the growing problem of the prairie farmers in respect of debt and credit and the very difficult economic situation which exists there. The minister did not refer specifically to farmers but I presume this procedure has been introduced in anticipation of the wider amendments so that the farmers may at least be able to stay afloat for a reasonable length of time.
The essential features are urgently needed. The individual will now be immune from legal proceedings and cannot be sued. I believe this is the essence of the matter. Individuals are also prohibited from contracting any debts above an amount of $500 until the consolidated debt is fully discharged. This feature indicates that the present action is merely a stopgap measure.
Because of the disastrous state of the economy at the present time, many Canadians have reached levels of credit or debt much larger than is provided for. If the situation is to be dealt with-and it comes directly under the responsibility of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs-something must be done by the government to control runaway inflation and to come to grips with the problem of growing unemployment. The people cannot live on debt and credit forever, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, the announcement
made by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs deals specifically with Part X of the Bankruptcy Act. As hon. members are aware, Part X was added to the Bankruptcy Act by Parliament in 1966 mainly at the request of the province of Manitoba and those provinces that had had orderly payment of debt legislation which had been found unconstitutional by the courts. When that request was granted in 1966 the action taken seemed to be appropriate, but it has now become clear that the level of debts is such that the ceiling must be raised.
We welcome the action of the minister in bringing in these regulations. However, I think this word could be added. If the wages, salaries and pensions of our people were a little better, and if we had a minister who would act aggressively on behalf of the consumers of this country, there would not be so much individual debt and we would not need this kind of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, the minister has just told the House that small wage earners who account for nearly 85 or 90 per cent of the population, are in debt, but I do not think that extending the scope of this legislation would prevent our small businesses and industries from going bankrupt.
Hon. members know that under the La-combe Act, which is in force in the province of Quebec and in other provinces throughout the country, low-income people can bring in to court part of their monthly, weekly or semi-monthly wages, which enables them to pay off their indebtedness over a number of years. But the minister will agree with me that if small wage earners have debts, it is precisely because they could not afford to pay cash. Here again, it is a matter of dollars and cents.
Under the present legislation, the small wage earner will be able to make payments to the court and, until he has paid all his debts, he will not be allowed to contract new ones above a level of $500 until the consolidated amount is fully repaid.
In other words, if a man is indebted for $1,500 for instance, he can undertake to repay $20 monthly and afterwards he will be
May 7, 1970



allowed to go into debt again, up to $500. The measure therefore is not likely to help the businessman or even the wage earner.
For instance, if a wage earner owes $200 or $300 to a small businessman and is allowed to repay his debt in monthly instalments of $10, $15 or $20, this will jeopardize the business of the small businessman who has extended credit. Now, under the new act, the government does not help the small businessman and will not be able to prevent bankruptcies. It is possible to keep an individual from going bankrupt. It is expensive for a man to declare bankruptcy, but it will cost him less to make monthly repayments. This is not, however, a solution to the present problem.
The minister clearly states that the problem in Canada is not one of production and purchase. The problem, in my opinion, is related to the repayment or payment of items bought. The Creditistes are quite aware of the problem and are suggesting to the government solutions which are not meant to drive everyone to bankruptcy, but to help everyone to become solvent following bankruptcies brought about by the government.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. Greene (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPLICATION OF PART VI, NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD ACT-AMENDMENTS TO REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to table a proclamation of the Governor in Council dated May 7, 1970, relating to Part VI of the National Energy Board Act. The proclamation was made by the Governor in Council in accordance with section 87(1) of the National Energy Board Act and I am tabling it at this time in accordance with section 87(4) of the Act.
Oil Policy
For the information of hon. members I am also tabling amendments to the National Energy Board Part VI regulations, which have the effect of limiting the application of controls under the Act to imports of motor gasoline into Canada, east of the province of Manitoba. The amendments also provide more complete reporting procedures for the importation and transfer of oil and oil products.
The purpose in making Part VI of the National Energy Board Act applicable to oil is to facilitate the enforcement of the national oil policy, which has now been in effect since 1961. As members know, the policy provides for markets west of the Ottawa Valley to be supplied substantially from Canadian crude. It is to the credit of the industry that the policy has worked well on a voluntary basis since its inception. However, it is now being jeopardized by the risk of increasing movements of foreign-origin product into Ontario west of the Ottawa Valley.
The western Canadian oil industry has flourished under the national oil policy to the well-being not only of western Canada but of the country as a whole, as all parts of Canada enjoy the downstream benefits of a thriving western Canadian oil industry. Therefore it is in the interests of all Canadians that the policy be maintained in order that the western Canadian oil industry may continue to thrive and prosper.
I would expect the National Energy Board to administer these new provisions in a manner which will result in non-disruption of supply and will provide for orderly and equitable conformity with the national oil policy.
Hon. D, S. Harkness (Calgary Centre): Mr. Speaker, I have neither the National Energy Board Act nor the regulations before me and thus am not able to determine what the actual effect of these changes will be. I am sorry that the minister did not make it very clear in his statement what the effect will be. If it is, as I hope, that the flow of gasoline and oil from foreign sources into the area west of the Ottawa Valley is now going to be effectively controlled, then this action certainly has my full support. I only regret that the government has been so long in taking steps in this direction. Several times during the past two or three years I have asked questions in the House concerning what action the National Energy Board and the government were prepared to take in order to prevent substantial importation of foreign gasoline

May 7, 1970
Oil Policy
and other petroleum products into the area west of the Ottawa River which was supposed to be reserved for Canadian oil, and up to date have never had satisfactory answers.
In his statement the minister says that the market in Ontario which is supposed to be reserved for western oil "is now being jeopardized by the risk of increasing movements of foreign-origin product into Ontario west of the Ottawa Valley." I must say that it has taken a long time for the government to wake up to a situation which has been one of very great concern to western oil producers for the past three years. The flow of foreign gasoline in particular into this area has been increasing at a very rapid rate for the last two years, and I fail to understand why the government has hesitated so long before taking action. However, as I said at the beginning, Mr. Speaker, I trust that the minister's announcement means that action is now to be taken to ensure that the provisions of the national oil policy are carried out.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPLICATION OF PART VI, NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD ACT-AMENDMENTS TO REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that the minister did not give us more information about the reasons for taking this step but I think it is predicated on two main theses. The first is that the national oil policy is becoming increasingly obsolete in light of the greatly increased capacity for oil production in western Canada. Hon. members will recall that under the original national oil policy western crude was to have a fairly free field in the American market. There was also to be a line of demarcation at the Ottawa River, and east of the Ottawa River offshore or foreign crude would enjoy most of the market. However, the increasing capacity for producing oil in western Canada made it necessary for the western oil industry to send more oil to the United States.
The second problem that has arisen is that the President of the United States recently imposed very rigid restrictions on the importation of Canadian oil into the western states of that country. I was glad to see that in a recent speech in Washington the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said that he thought the President's decision in that regard was a mistake.
The action now being taken by the government would appear to be in response to the President's decision in order to safeguard
[Mr. Harkness.J
some of the markets in eastern Canada for western crude. It may help to some extent, but I suggest to the minister that there should be a complete revision of the national oil policy very soon. For a long time we in this party have urged the minister to use all the powers at his disposal to extend the oil pipeline east to Montreal so that Canadian crude can have the eastern market in order to allow oil wells in western Canada to operate at a much higher capacity than at the present time.
The immediate step which the minister has taken to in an attempt to resolve the situation certainly will not be the complete solution. We look forward to the minister making a fuller statement and introducing a revised national oil policy in the near future.

-the enforcement of the national oil policy which has now been in effect since 1961.
The national oil policy is now being jeopardized by the risk of increasing movements of foreign-origin products into Ontario west of the Ottawa Valley.

Mr. Speaker, as the leader of the New Democratic party (Mr. Douglas) said earlier, we feel the government must take steps and revise the law, if necessary, in order to protect our natural resources and their development in the interest of Canadians.
We do not suggest to cease all foreign trade, far from it, but the prime concern of a government should be to make sure that our industries and the Canadian people benefit as much as possible from the development of our natural resources.
Therefore, we support the action taken by the government. It may be a little late but,
I repeat, better late than never.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in the debate on Bill C-197, entitled "An Act to establish the National Farm Products Marketing Council and to authorize the establishment of national marketing agencies for farm products."
I shall say right away that this legislation will exert an absolute control over the entire farm economy, and add that the Liberals have certainly not been elected to bring in a socialist system, but to protect democracy. This government should administer instead of poking its nose in the economic system of the country.
Of course, if citizens did not exist, there would be no government. The raison d'etre of the government is to protect the individuals, not to enslave them. I do not know why the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) who is familiar with economics and who studied the principles of freedom and security wishes to impose such legislation that will put agriculture under the yoke. Farmers will no longer have any responsibility. They will be treated as mere things. What is the policy of the government? It has no right to create socialist organizations and to force them unto the Canadian people.

Today more than ever, to meet the aspirations of the people, efforts are made, with good reason, to raise the level of agricultural and industrial production as well as the volume of services. This is why we must encourage technical progress, the innovating mind, the creation and extension of industries.
For several years, the provincial and federal governments have been asking farmers to increase their production and to modernize their equipment. For that purpose, farm loans were granted. We were told that the Canadian government and people needed an increased production and that farmers should modernize their equipment further. The farmers have fully complied with the requests of the federal and provincial governments.
The farmers are now penalized, because they have a surplus production. All kinds of restrictions are laid down, because there is an excess of production. We did the same thing from 1929 to 1939 when the governments were requesting people to go back to the farm, forcing city people to open and cultivate new farmlands and so increase the national heritage. At that time politicians were supposed to have foresight. After having done all this, today we will oblige these same farmers who brought these lands into cultivation at the price of immense sacrifice and privation to leave them. We are telling them to go back to the city. Policies today are different from those of yore which are no longer acceptable. Your farms are not paying their way as they do not yield 10, 12 or 15 per cent interest for finance companies, so you have to leave them and go back to the city. There you are invited to live on social welfare and the government will rob the workers so that you might continue to subsist.
That is the present situation of agriculture. The Minister of Agriculture is well aware of the harm done to this industry in the last few years. He knows also that, in many areas, from 50 to 70 per cent of the farmers have left their farms. How is it that farm policy was effective 25 or 30 years ago, while today those same farms cannot support the farmers' families?

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL MARKETING COUNCIL AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not very often that I am introduced to the House by a Credi-
6690	COMMONS
Farm Products Marketing Agencies Bill tiste, but I accept the proposition. I have been studying certain aspects of this bill and I must say in all frankness that it does cause me a good deal of concern. I am very much aware of the problem the bill purports to tackle. It purports to make provision for marketing aids, plans and structures that are national in scope. The purpose is to overcome difficulties faced under provincial marketing arrangements because frequently it is impossible or very difficult to arrange for orderly marketing within a province in view of the fact a province cannot control what comes in either from some other province or from some other country. The result is that markets in a province can be flooded, and the efforts of a provincial marketing organization can be negated or very seriously damaged.
I think we are all familiar with this problem. Certainly, anyone who has been associated with provincial governments or with farm organizations would be very familiar with this problem. What disturbs me about the bill, however, is that it places Canadian agriculture and the Canadian farmer very much under the control of the government of Canada. The bill attacks the problem but it does so with vengeance. It seems to me that it takes the Canadian farmer out of the frying pan but puts him right into the fire. It purports to answer the pleas for help from farmers in respect of orderly marketing by the government itself, directly and through agencies, taking control of the supply, processing and marketing of any agricultural product other than those products regulated by the Canadian Wheat Board or the Dairy Commission. In other words, the control under this bill is to be taken away from the farmers, the farm organizations and provincial marketing organizations and placed entirely in the hands of the federal government and federal government agencies.
The government is asking for power to exercise full control, either itself or through agencies which come under its control. As members of the House will know, the bill now provides for the appointment of a National Farm Products Marketing Council which would have power to study and recommend in respect of the establishment of forums or agencies to control one or more particular farm products. The council would have the authority to supervise the operation of these agencies. The members of the National Farm Products Marketing Council are to be appointed by the Governor in Council. There is no indication of who is to be

DEBATES	May 7, 1970
represented, if anybody. The Governor in Council is to be given a very free hand in the selection of members of the National Farm Products Marketing Council. As I read the bill, it would seem that these members are to be appointed at pleasure and presumably could be removed at the pleasure of the government. It would appear to be really a governmental-departmental agency.
The bill urges, and indeed instructs, that public officials are to be used by the council and I believe also by its agencies to the fullest extent possible in its work. It would seem, therefore, to be very likely that this marketing council will in fact be staffed, so far as advice and information is concerned, by governmental employees. There is nothing wrong with governmental employees so far as that is concerned, but of course they are not a part of farm organizations and do not in any way represent the points of view of farm organizations.
The bill also makes provision for the National Farm Products Marketing Council to hold hearings. As I see it, there is no provision in the bill for any participation by farm organizations and producers of a particular commodity or for a guarantee in respect of participation in the reaching of a decision. Indeed, there would seem to be no provision for consultation except the provision relating to the holding of hearings. As I read the bill, it would not seem to be compulsory that the council should even hold hearings before making recommendations to the Governor in Council with regard to a marketing structure for a particular commodity.
Certainly, there is no requirement for meaningful farm consultation or consent. So far as that is concerned, sir, there is really no assurance of consumer protection. There is a pious declaration that the council and presumably the agencies will take into consideration the consumer interest, but there is no structural provision either to protect the farmer or the consumer. On both counts, the discretion is to be left entirely with the Governor in Council. I really do not believe this is a statement which can be disputed. I am not talking about what the intentions of the minister might be, but rather about the intentions of the government. There is no structure in this bill that would ensure consultation with the farmers or protection for the consumer. The Governor in Council is given the authority to establish an agency to control the supply and marketing of any agricultural product, with the two exceptions mentioned in
May 7, 1970	COMMONS
the bill. This control continues right down the line from growing to processing, packaging and marketing. This is a very far-reaching bill.
It would seem to be very clear that if this bill becomes law the government, through the Governor in Council, would be able to impose its views and its decisions upon Canadian farmers, upon Parliament and upon the country without requiring anybody else's opinion, certainly not that of Parliament. I believe the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) gave assurances to the joint convention of the Farmers Union of Alberta and the Alberta Federation of Agriculture on March 24. I do not like to suggest that the minister was not frank at that time. I would prefer to say that he was perhaps mistaken. On that day he said this to that joint convention:
National marketing agencies will not be set until it is demonstrated that there is a wide producer consensus on the needs for them. It will not be the role of government alone to actively work for and organize that consensus. It will require the assistance of the producers themselves through their organizations, such as this one.
We are creating the machinery. It will be up to the producers to use it.
With careful planning, national marketing agencies represent, I feel, an opportunity for Canadian producers to get together for stable, orderly marketing, of their products. That they will work only with your support.
Now, it may very well be the intention of the minister that national marketing agencies will not be set up until it has been demonstrated that there is a wide producer consensus concerning the need for them; that may be the minister's present intention and it may continue to be his intention while he is Minister of Agriculture. However, I do not know this and I do not think he can give us any assurance concerning his future intentions. The point is that, as I read the bill, there is nothing in it to ensure that what he told this joint convention in Alberta will in fact be so. There is nothing in the bill to ensure that these agencies will be set up only after it has been demonstrated there is a consensus among producers regarding the need for them. There is nothing in the bill to require anyone to consult the farmers about anything.

speechtext:
There is no provision for producer control. Mr. Munro of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture accepted a kind of supply management that is entirely different from the structure proposed by the government in this bill. I will quote what Mr. Munro said, and it will not be out of context. I will give the whole quotation to the minister, who is probably familiar with it. Mr. Munro stated:
But farmers want to keep their business in their hands as this process moves forward. They want to determine, for themselves, the choices that are made among the often hard alternatives that face them. They want to remain independent producers working with other farmers.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture stated on April 9, 1970 in its brief to the government that there should be:
-a positive program of agricultural adjustment-implemented without authoritarian policy and procedures-and which would give farmers opportunities to improve their situation.
I submit that this is exactly what this bill does not do. There is no reason at all to believe that a bill as authoritarian as this, a bill that concentrates so much power in the hands of the minister and of his colleagues in the government, and a bill that gives the farmers of this country so little say in what is going to happen to them, would have any widespread support in the country, in the farming or any other community. It is highly centralized in its control. There is good reason to worry about it.
As I said, the bill is authoritarian. Consider the significance of this bill for the many existing provincially authorized but producer controlled boards. Consider the power that will be exercised through the control of imports which may be delegated to one of these agencies by the Governor in Council. Consider the effect on these provincial boards that such an agency may exercise through control of inter-provincial trade. I do not think it is exaggerating to say that very frequently at least one of these agencies would be able to bring any provincially authorized board to its knees. In any event, if this bill is

adopted in its present form, the effect will be that producers in Canada will have less say about marketing in Canada than they have today.

The minister says that is absolutely wrong. The existing boards will have less influence. In fact, so far as this bill is concerned, they will have no say in connection with the agencies that may control the marketing of produce on a national scale. Certainly, there is nothing in the bill to prevent this from happening. We have only to look at the Canadian Dairy Commission which was established to help an industry. We all recognize that it is exercising far-reaching control, that it virtually has power of life and death over those in the dairy business. We know that thousands and thousands of people have gone out of the dairy business as a result of its regulations, not because of anything parliament decided but because of the particular way in which that commission has exercised the power delegated to it.
If anybody thinks that the minister and the government will go gingerly in the exercise of the power conferred by this bill, that person has only to consider the LIFT program. One can see how, under that program, the quotas established under the Canadian Wheat Board are being used to enforce not voluntary cuts but really what are compulsory cuts in production.
Another defect in this bill is that it contains nothing but very general statements of objectives. The government's own task force warned the government as follows:
It is dangerous to advocate a program of supply control without being specific about the kind of administration, the techniques of control and the initial allocation and transfer of quotas which must be an integral part of such a program. Questions such as the inter-provincial allocation of quotas, transferability of quotas among producers, and many other similar considerations dealt with in detail in the main body of this report have a profound bearing on the success or otherwise of such a program.
But what does the bill really say about the goals to be achieved? What does it say about the use of quotas? What does it say about the allocation of quotas? Will these be allocated on the basis of out-put at the present time or over a period of time? Are they to be allocated in terms of productive capacity or in some other way, and upon what terms are they to

Farm Products Marketing Agencies Bill be transferable? Obviously, these are very important questions, and they will be left entirely in the hands of a commission or agency, or of the Governor in Council. The farmers themselves will have nothing to say about them. These questions are of enormous importance to Canadian farmers, but there is not the slightest assurance in the bill that they will have any say about them.
The quota system which is adopted and the way in which it is handled are surely basic,, because if the system is handled in a particular way it could perpetuate inefficiency, it could perpetuate vested interests in agriculture, it could have the effect of keeping young people from getting into farming, and certainly it could hurt national productivity. Yet Members of Parliament are asked to delegate to the government this blanket authority, really requiring the government to consult no one unless it is supposed to consult this commission consisting of its own appointees. We cannot assume that the farmers will approve of this.
How much emphasis is to be put on marketing? How much emphasis is to be put on developing markets as opposed to controlling supply? I would think that if the farmers are given an effective voice in establishing and directing these agencies there would be some assurance that a lot of emphasis would be placed on marketing, because farmers will want to expand their production; but there is absolutely no assurance that an agency, run by a group of appointees, perhaps assisted by bureaucrats, would have any interest in doing anything else but in keeping out of trouble.
What about the consumer? So far as the consumer is concerned I suggest that this commission, and these corporations established under the Governor in Council, will be pretty well beyond the effective surveillance of Parliament. They will be inclined to go their own sweet way and Parliament will have a devil of a time getting at them at all, or exercising any influence over them either from the point of view of the farmer or of the consumer.
Surely, here we have another example of the grasping efforts of the government to get more power. It is quite in line with the attacks on the Auditor General. It is quite in line with the establishment of Information Canada. Here, we see the government trying to concentrate great power in a particular field, perhaps delegated to agencies but not agencies which are independent. After all, the CRTC has some independence from the gov-

Surely, this House and the people of Canada are getting a bellyfull of the efforts of the government to concentrate excessive power in its own hands.
I do not oppose the principle of the bill. I understand the need for efficient, effective national marketing agencies. I understand the weakness in the present situation. I understand the need for farmers to have stronger and more effective marketing agencies in the face of the competition they have to meet. But, Mr. Speaker, we must curb the power of the government. We must ensure that the farmers have an effective voice in the marketing of their produce. Surely, we have not reached the point in this country where the control of all farm produce-growing it, processing it, packaging it and marketing it-is to be concentrated in the hands of the Governor in Council as represented by the Minister of Agriculture? This is a magnificent concentration of authority and power.
The minister may assure us that he will administer it with beneficence. I do not know that. We are considering legislation, and this legislation is authoritarian. It is dictatorial. Unless it is changed it must be fought, because I have not got that much faith in the benefits of this centralization of power. I have not got that much faith in the benefits of government planning in this centralized and authoritarian way. I have too much respect for Canadian farmers to tie them to the government's apron strings in this way and make them subject to the tender mercies of the government. Granted that there is need for more effective marketing machinery, I say to the minister in all sincerity that as drafted this bill would destroy Canadian farming as we know it. It would destroy the enterprise of Canadian farmers as we know it. Somehow or other, if we cannot get some sense into the minister we must get some sense into the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I find the debate on Bill C-197 most Interesting. If the minister is so dedicated to protecting the rights of farmers, and making sure that any marketing arrangement is set up only with their consent and advice, why is he so ambiguous and so indefinite in the provisions which the bill proposes? If his only justification for saying that there is ample provision for consultation with the farmers is

clause 8, the first of which line reads, "A public hearing shall be held by the council", then he is not consistent. In fact, it seems to me that the minister is being less than frank about Bill C-197. I do not question his motives. I believe if he were to administer the bill he would endeavour to see it was properly enforced, but he will not be the Minister of Agriculture forever and not everybody in his department may feel as he does about it. It seems to me that some of his senior officials have had a lot more to do with drafting it than he has. I cannot believe he would ever draft a bill like this himself. I have too much respect for his convictions, as I used to understand them, to feel that he would intentionally be a party to this. I think it would be keeping faith with the farmers, if not with his colleagues in the House, and even members on this side of the House, if some of the things which he must realize are not the way he wants them were changed.
To say a public hearing will guarantee the right of a farmer to participate in any marketing agency set up is ridiculous. It is of little comfort that public hearings can be held prior to the establishment of marketing agencies or plans for those agencies. Public hearings are not one of the checks in our political system and such hearings do not have to be held if the minister and the marketing council do not wish to hold them. Certainly, they cannot represent and do not represent the opinion of the majority of farmers.
If the minister is as determined that farmers be consulted as he says he is, why does he not make specific provision for that in the bill? Why leave it as it stands? Certainly, the provision for consultation by this proposed national marketing agency is inadequate. In fact, at the Joint Convention of the Farmers Union of Alberta and the Alberta Federation of Agriculture on March 24 last. The minister of Agriculture stated:
National marketing agencies will not be set until it is demonstrated that there is a wide producer consensus on the needs for them.
If this is his conviction, why does the bill not make that clear? In my opinion, this bill in no way allows for adequate consultation.
What does "producer consensus" mean anyway? The Minister stated, at that same meeting:
We are creating the machinery. It will be up to the producers to use it.
It is true that he is creating the machinery but it will be up to the producers to use it, whether they like it or not. This whole aspect

is misleading. When the Minister speaks about "consensus" and "requests of a substantial majority of producers" as a criteria for establishing marketing agencies and the structure of such agencies, he is expressing popular sentiments but not describing the black and white statute power he is asking for in Bill C-197.
This is why I am concerned about this bill.
I wish more people were concerned. I do not see many members of the government in the House and only one member of the Press Gallery-and I have great respect for the person who is faithfully making notes. Agriculture is still one of the vital, basic industries of this country and if we do not pay more attention to the preservation of what has made our agricultural industry the most efficient and most effective agricultural industry in the world, it is going to be something less than it is at the present time.
I am in favour of producer sponsored marketing boards. It is imperative, in the situation where the farmer cannot control and cannot plan or arrange for adequate marketing facilities, that there be marketing boards. But the majority of producers must want them and help determine how they are to be administered, not have them foisted upon them. I am convinced, in spite of what the minister says, that this is the effect of this bill. It is not good enough for the minister to express his intentions here in the House and in other places. The bill has got to substantiate those intentions and it does not, Mr. Speaker.
The producers do not have any provision for proper representation in connection with the setting up of such agencies. I was equally amazed a little while ago when the minister said this is provided in Clause 31 of the bill. There is nothing in that Clause that refers to producers. In fact, the word producers is not used. The bill does indicate, however, a farmer may be put in jail for two years if he does not co-operate with the inspectors. It is at this point where the "producer" is specifically referred to. Clause 34 reads:

(3) The owner or person in charge of any place referred to in subsection (1) and every person found therein shall give an inspector all reasonable assistance in his power to enable the inspector to carry out his duties and functions under this act and shall furnish him with such information with respect to any regulated product found therein as he may reasonably require.

(1) Every person who violates any provision of this act or of a marketing plan that an agency is authorized to implement or who fails to comply with a requirement of the council pursuant to paragraph (e) of section 7 is guilty of

That is where the farmer comes in, Mr. Speaker. It seems to me that the Minister, and again I express my respect for him, is more interested in implementing the basic policies of the government to which he belongs than he is in presenting the opinions of the western farmer and his problems to the cabinet of which he is a part. This is where the western farmer is being left out. I only wish there was a voice in the cabinet, and I expected there would be when the Minister became part of it, that would speak for the farmer and the particular area of agriculture in the west with which both of us are so familiar. Instead of that, the Minister tries to justify and explain the policies of his government to the people who live on farms and who are the producers of agricultural products in this country. It is one thing to tell the farmer what the minister or the government thinks is good for him and it is another thing to sit down with the farmer and work out answers to problems. It seems to me this is where the hon. minister is falling short of his responsibilities.

Farm Products Marketing Agencies Bill [DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Let us return to the question of marketing agencies. Generally, the same form of marketing institution is desired by everyone. However, this bill represents a specific type of farm marketing legislation and in my opinion does not have nor ever will have the general support of the farm community. This bill frees the government to, by itself, authoritatively regulate all aspects of food production, distribution and marketing. It invites central and statist administration with an all-pervasive scope over supply and market management. That is what the government is asking for, but that is not what the farmers and agricultural economists have been considering. In my opinion, that is not what the minister has been saying in the House and throughout the country to the various organizations involved with agriculture, and that is why we are concerned about the bill.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture stated on April 9 of this year, in its annual brief to the government, that there should be a positive program of agricultural adjustment, implemented without authoritarian policies and procedures, which would give farmers opportunities to improve their situation. I wish this bill did just that. It seems to me that Bill C-197 could be used to attack the very process of governing that is being practiced by the present government. Essentially, the present government and the government it took over from worked on the assumption that governments can best solve national problems; but they have refused to put into statute form their national goals or state their conclusions as to how to reach these goals. The range of choices, and they are hard choices, Mr. Speaker, is left to the bureaucracy and the substance of their legislation is little more than catalogues of sentiment or a pathological delegation of power. It is, putting it simply, bureaucratic statism, because the bill contains no philosophy; it outlines no strategy and shows an inclination to leave these problems to the secret structure of government. That is why we are afraid. We have seen what has happened with the Wheat Board and the Dairy Commission.
These bodies, set up originally to serve farmers, are now viewed by them with deep suspicion. In fact, the hon. member for Pallis-er (Mr. Schumacher) recently conducted a poll in his constituency, his being basically a rural constituency, in which he asked the farmers what they thought about the Wheat

Board. The majority of farmers participating in the poll said they were dissatisfied and suspicious of it. Yet the board was established to serve the farmers. Legislative guidelines left the government the freedom of choosing goals and strategies for the Wheat Board and I fear that the same will apply in this case.
Another objection I have is that the bill does not declare government policy. Supply and market management can be a boon or a disaster for agriculture and the national interest. The results depend on the goals to be achieved and the strategies to be employed. These are difficult questions and Parliament has no right, in an open democracy, to delegate their arbitration to the cabinet and the federal bureaucracy that serves it. The government task force on agriculture made this quite clear when it said:
It is dangerous to advocate a program of supply control without being specific about the kind of administration, the techniques of control and the initial part of such a program. Questions such as the inter-provincial allocation of quotas, transferability of quotas among producers, and many other similar considerations dealt with in detail in the main body of this report have a profound bearing on the success or otherwise of such a program.
This bill does not even refer to goals that the minister said the government intends to reach. Neither does it enlarge on the more elaborate strategies to be employed. There is another serious question that the bill in no way answers, the question of income for farmers. Farm income constitutes a grave problem in all Canada today. Owing to the cost-price squeeze, a farmer's income is barely enough to meet his operating expenses, leaving him with nothing on which to live. The bill does not say whether the goal of the legislation is the stabilization of farm income or the increasing of farm income by supply management. This is immensely important. It is very debatable whether supply management can efficiently, effectively, fairly do both. I might point out that the task force speaks about this matter very clearly.
We have attacked Bill C-197 for its irresponsible ambivalence. According to the minister, it can do all things. However, viewing the vivid trend of this government's agricultural policy, as revealed in the Wheat Board and Dairy Commission administration, we ought to be quite certain how this bill will, over a period of time, be interpreted in the closed halls of this government. That is one reason we are opposing it. It seems to me that this bill, Bill C-197, completes the Prime
May 7, 1970

Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) statute power to undertake the policy of "adjustment". We believe that Bill C-197 indicates quite clearly that the degree of power sought by the government is far in excess of that proposed in any reviews of the agricultural industry, and those powers would usurp completely the control now vested in the hands of the primary producers. This could prove dangerous.
In this regard, Mr. Speaker, the minister has said that he will consult and work with present agencies, particularly those of provincial governments; yet there is nothing in this legislation which says he must. This legislation will set up agencies which supersede entirely existing agencies, whether sponsored by farm or provincial organizations.
I have not heard the minister talk about this and am concerned.
I wish to make a few remarks about the general agricultural situation, because it seems to me that this bill will set the pattern for what is to take place across the entire agricultural picture in this country. Our primary producers, and primary producers all over the world, are the victims of a revolution which is progressively eliminating small producers and forcing them to live at a lower standard. Skilful propaganda is urging us to abandon the traditional concepts of farming and to adopt the idea that there must be a progressive centralization of farming and scientific control. The truth is that behind such programs for progressive centralizing of farm production lies the long term objective of eliminating the individual, primary producer. I see it is five o'clock, Mr. Speaker. If I were allowed two or three minutes extra, I could finish my remarks.

speechtext:
that Bill S-22, to incorporate National Farmers Union, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills and Standing Orders.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to introduce this bill, S-22, in the House of Commons. In doing so I should like to give the House a little background to the matter.
As members may know, most companies in Canada now become incorporated under the Canada Corporation Act. However, because that act does not cover the situation where the incorporation involves an amalgamation of companies already incorporated in one or more provinces, as is the case with the National Farmers Union, it is necessary to proceed by way of a private bill.
Certain individuals, named in clause 1 of this bill, plus some existing farm organizations, have expressed a desire for a national farmers organization, to be known as the National Farmers Union, and they have prepared this bill which is now known as Bill S-22, the legislation having been first introduced in the other place. It was investigated by a committee there and was given third reading with no amendments.
The objects of the proposed National Farmers Union are set out in clause 3 of the Bill and are as follows:
- (a) to promote the betterment of farmers in the attainment of their economic and social goals;
(b)	to conduct projects for the benefit of farmers in the development of markets for and marketing of farm products;
(c)	to achieve the reduction of costs and other measures designed to increase the economic benefits of farming;
(d)	to conduct educational and research projects for the benefit of farmers;
(e)	to promote and secure legislation and other forms of government action for the benefit of farmers;
(f)	to promote a higher standard of community life in agriculture; and
(g)	to promote services for its members consistent with its objects and work jointly with any other persons or organizations for the attainment of its objects.
I believe hon. members will agree that these objectives are desirable and that the
Private Bills
House should give them its blessing by giving speedy and favourable consideration to this Bill.
Farmers in Canada have always had great difficulty in organizing themselves in an effective way. It is important in our highly organized society that all segments be equally well equipped to protect their own interests; otherwise, the weak and the unorganized tend to be left behind in the economic race. Therefore, I believe we should encourage the National Farmers Union by accommodating its desire to be incorporated on a national basis. There have been provincial farmers union groups for many years, which in turn have had a type of loose arrangement with each other, which apparently was not as successful as the members would have wished. This National Farmers Union is something that was overwhelmingly approved by a nation-wide convention last summer in Winnipeg.

maintopic: S701 PRIVATE BILLS AGRICULTURE MEASURE TO INCORPORATE NATIONAL FARMERS UNION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a few words concerning Bill S-22.1 realize there is a great deal of need for farmers across the nation being organized so that they might have power in the market place and so that they, too, may be able to exercise some degree of power in respect of the marketing of their products. I am slightly amazed, however, that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas) is the sponsor of this bill. I know that lawyers on occasion must present bills and act as consultants. I know, too, that everybody is entitled to a defence and a fair hearing. I suppose any and every organization across Canada is entitled to have somebody

May 7, 1970
Private Bills
present a bill on their behalf to incorporate something, as is the case in respect of Bill S-22.
I must say, however, that I believe the National Farmers Union to be a divisive organization among farmers. It may seem strange that I would say this organization divides and not unites. The very title of the bill states that this organization is a national farmers union and after reading the title one would be inclined to believe that this organization would tend to unite farmers. The fact is that this organization really is dividing the farmers. Members of the National Farmers Union go across the country fighting with other farm organizations. For some time there has been a strong farm organization in Alberta. In fact, if one were to make a comparison at the provincial level in respect of membership one would easily see that the Alberta farmers organization has had a greater membership than the Saskatchewan Farmers Union which, in essence, is the union that is the foundation for the National Farmers Union.
The National Farmers Union, which by means of this bill would be incorporated nationally, has had representatives in Alberta vigorously competing against the organization which the farmers in Alberta have accepted as their voice. The Alberta Farmers Union is amalgamated with the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and has given Alberta one strong farm voice. The new organization is called "Unifarm". The national farm organization has been campaigning against Unifarm. So, it is actually dividing rather than uniting the farmers. I say we should examine the situation before we incorporate such a farm body. Let us examine the purpose of a national farm organization. Is it to gather together farmers from all across Canada, in all facets of agriculture, so that they may lobby more effectively in Ottawa? Let us suppose that such a national organization wishes to lobby at the provincial government level. Let us also ask ourselves whether a national farm organization could lobby better at the provincial level than could a provincial farm organization.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the House that in my estimation a body which speaks for the farmers of a particular province, whether it be Prince Edward Island, Saskatchewan, Alberta or any province in Canada, can lobby more effectively with a provincial government if it is a provincial organization. Why should premiers or minis-

ters of agriculture be interested or concerned about the voice of a national organization which may or may not purport to help certain segments of the industry within a particular province? Why should they listen to that organization when they can and may well listen to the voice of a provincial organization within the particular province? If members would think about this for a moment, I believe they would realize that a provincial farm body could lobby more effectively before a provincial government than could a national farm body.
In considering this bill to incorporate the National Farmers Union, I say that we must concern ourselves with the question of whether a national farm body can lobby more effectively on behalf of the farmers at the national level than can a group of provincial farm organizations. It is a coincidence that Bill S-22 is before us at the same time that Bill C-197 is before us. One may ask how I draw the parallel and where the concern is. Bill C-197 is new federal legislation to introduce into Canada-and I might say whether Canadians want it or not-a national marketing council. This marketing council will have power to establish marketing agencies which will have power to control and handle one commodity. Each agency will handle production, transportation, selling, packaging and the pricing of that commodity. I should like members of the House to consider this aspect. We have before us now legislation in respect of the setting up of marketing agencies within provincial boundaries. If hon. members have followed my argument up until now they will have reached the conclusion that a provincial farmers union can lobby more effectively at the provincial level.
Now, we are to set up by Bill C-197 marketing agencies which in 99 out of 100 cases will in essence have control over production, transportation, packaging, pricing and selling of a commodity within a provincial boundary. So, it would appear to me that a provincial farmers union, in the years ahead, might well have more power and more influence and might well have more say at the market level in respect of the produce of the farms than would a national farm body. If a national farm boby wants to become a political party or a national association, that is one thing. But if it wants to be concerned with the plight of the farmers and the marketing of the farmers' products, I say to this House and to you, Mr. Speaker, that a provincial farmers union in the years ahead, in the 1970's, may
May 7, 1970

bring about more actual, concrete good tor the farmers than such a national union.
9 (5:30 p.m.)
Let us consider the concept of the National Farmers Union organizing on a national scale to defend all farmers' causes. It is like motherhood-everybody is for it. As a farmer from western Canada I should, perhaps, automatically support it because farmers have to unite; they have to organize and defend themselves. No one else will do that for them;
I agree with this. However, we must realize that the problems of the 1960's may well become the frustrations of the 1970's, in light of the fact that under Bill C-197 marketing agencies and a marketing council will be set up to deal in particular with commodities. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the House that in the years ahead commodity organizations and farm commodity groups may be far more important.
I see the hon. member for Assiniboia is nodding his head in agreement with what I am saying. I am pleased to see that, because I wondered why the hon. member should sponsor the bill. However, I do not hold it against him because, as I said previously, lawyers have to accept both bad and good cases and, I suppose, someone has to sponsor a bill to incorporate the National Farmers Union. Why it fell upon the hon. member to do so, I am not sure; but I see he is nodding his head in agreement with what I have said, that because of the marketing legislation the emphasis will be placed on the commodity groups, not on an across-the-board National Farmers Union.
How can a wheat farmer who is president of the National Farmers Union defend the potato industry in Prince Edward Island? I ask that question, Mr. Speaker, and my answer to it is: Not very well. How can the president of the National Farmers Union who is a Saskatchewan wheat farmer defend vegetable producers in Brooks, an area with which both the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and I are familiar. The answer to that question is also: Not very well.
So while I know that everyone should support a farmers' union, and everyone agrees with the concept that farmers should unite and organize-it is like upholding motherhood-I do not support this piece of legislation and I do not support the National Farmers Union because I think it is an organization of the past. It is being incorporated too late. Perhaps 35 years ago, before the formation of
Private Bills
the Wheat Board, the incorporation of this organization would have been justified. But perhaps not even then would it have been justified.
Farmers must organize into commodity groups. Although I do not approve of, and will not support Bill C-197, on which I will speak later provided we clear away some of the other problems confronting this House, I am sufficiently realistic to know that the Minister of Agriculture, rightly or wrongly, will push through Bill C-197 which may well become the law of the land. I will certainly move an amendment to it and I hope it will be accepted because I know it expresses a principle which the Minister of Agriculture espoused when he used to sit to my left.
In any case, I am sufficiently realistic to accept the fact that Bill C-197 may well become the law of the land. If it is to become the law of the land, then farmers all across the country had better organize their commodity groups and become concerned with the marketing, handling, pricing, transportation and packaging of the commodities which they produce.
The National Farmers Union will be the crying receptacle of all farmers in all plights. However, it will deal with no particular commodity nor will it be able to lend support to the producers of any one commodity. So I say to the sponsor of the bill and to the National Farmers Union that they are 30 years too late and that in the years ahead the whole emphasis will be on commodity unions within provincial farm organizations, because the agencies set up under the marketing council will tend to be within provincial boundaries and therefore a particular case for a commodity can be better argued within that provincial boundary and a better lobby can be organized by farmers with a strong provincial organization.
I have expressed some of the thoughts that have passed through my mind in reading Bill S-22, to incorporate the National Farmers Union. I might say openly and without intending to offend that I am surprised the hon. member for Assiniboia is sponsoring this bill. This is a piece of legislation which would be more appropriately sponsored by the party to my left which has sponsored farmers unions in the past and is more inclined to agree with them. But again I have to admit that there is not very much difference between the government party and the party

to my left, so perhaps I should not be surprised that the hon. member for Assiniboia is supporting the bill.

It seems to me that this bill gives the National Farmers Union far too much power and this emphasis is misplaced when one considers that the problems of the 1960's may become the frustrations of the 1970's, particularly with respect to the agricultural community if Bill C-197 passes and if farmers are allowed to organize under the provisions of Bill S-22 at the national level, when the emphasis should really be on the formation of provincial commodity groups.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I think that Bill S-22 should not be passed by this House because it is poor legislation. Farmers should be given time to consider all the aspects of Bill S-22. They should be given time in which to be encouraged to join commodity groups and strong provincial farm unions. I do not believe that Bill S-22 should pass tonight, particularly prior to the passage of Bill C-197, because Bill C-197 will also affect the role of a farmers union. Farmers

need more time in which to consider the powers that the National Farmers Union is seeking through this bill.
While I do not condemn the farmers for joining the National Farmers Union-they are grasping at every straw they can-I say to this House that the National Farmers Union is not the answer. Farmers have to organize strongly provincially, and strongly commodity-wise. This is the way by which their case can be better argued with legislatures and better presented through the marketing agencies that have been developed.
There is no question that in today's society all power rests with the chain stores. Somebody once told me there are 27 major chain stores in Canada which really control the pricing, packaging and selling of farm produce. For that matter, they also control the transportation of agricultural commodities. These commodity groups, these chain stores in many cases operate under provincial legislation; their operations take place within the boundaries of a province. Therefore, I believe that farmers must become strong at the commodity level and at the provincial level in order to safeguard their rights of production, their rights of marketing, their rights of pricing and of selling their produce.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCORPORATE NATIONAL FARMERS UNION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take a great deal of time on this bill but I do want to give it my full support. As a past president of the National Farmers Union I spent considerable time in various provinces promoting the organizing of farmers so that the National Farmers Union could effectively speak on their behalf. This is really what this bill permits farmers to do-to speak on their own behalf, and nothing more.
Mention has been made of the tremendous powers that this bill will give to the organization concerned. What the bill does is give the National Farmers Union the right and the status to operate on a national basis. At this point in time it is idle to speculate what type of organization will represent farmers in the future. It is wrong to say that the National Farmers Union is an organization of the past rather than of the future. This type of organization could hardly have been possible 30 years ago because communications at that time did not permit of the concept of farmers across the country gathering at national conventions to decide their future and to decide the course of action they would pursue. We have moved into an era where we have transportation in terms of aircraft and communication in terms of radio, television and telephone which permit the concept of a national farmers organization through which farmers across the country can meet annually, or at such other times as they may choose, to set out the policy to be followed by their organization.
With present day transportation, fresh vegetables can move from California to Montreal, Toronto or Saskatchewan markets overnight and arrive almost as fresh as when they left. With present-day transportation, hogs are moved back and forth across the country with the result that prices for them are established almost simultaneously in all areas. With modern transportation, the price of potatoes in P.E.I. is relevant to the price of potatoes in Alberta or Manitoba.
If farmers are to deal effectively with the circumstances that face them in the 1970's their organizations must be geared to meet conditions on a national level. This is why Bill C-197 takes the same basic approach. Farmers are in desperate straits, and I do not know why a member of this House would
Private Bills
stand up and try to deny them the right to take action such as is proposed in this bill, iwhich only gives them the right to do what other organizations are already doing, be those other organizations Imperial Oil, the labour unions or the medical profession. All this bill says to farmers is that if they have the willingness and if they will put up the money, they can do the same things as these other organizations.
I personally know many of the men and women whose names are mentioned in this bill, who devote their time, efforts and money to achieve the betterment of farmers. With respect to those who wish to question the motives of this organization, I leave it to them to substantiate the questions they raise. That they can do on the hustings. I support this bill with all the earnestness that I can.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the name National Farmers Union is somewhat misleading, if hon. members think that this represents a consensus of the farmers of Canada.

speechtext:
I am making clear that it does not. The reason is quite plain. It has been debated for years, certainly ever since I had anything to do with farming, and I was born on a farm. I am sure that the sponsor of the bill and both hon. gentlemen who followed him will agree that it is most difficult by interpretation or by definition to say what is a farmer, let alone to say what is an average farmer, what is a family farmer or what is any particular type of farmer. Within farm unions from time to time there have been long and heated arguments about whether their programs and objectives represent the average farmer or a proper percentage of farmers.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Even if you had the consensus of a majority of the farm unions of Alberta you would only be representing a percentage of one particular group of people, those who think that the farm union of Alberta, now called Unifarm, represents in the democratic sense the majority of farmers. As legislators we have great difficulty. Unless we look into the question very carefully, with the best intentions we might pass legislation thinking it was in accordance with the wishes of the average farmer. By taking a poll which shows a 68 per cent vote of the farm union of Alberta, if

May 7. 1970
Private Bills
you did not know any better you could assume you were legislating for 68 per cent of the farmers of Alberta. But this would be a false assumption. Farmers themselves find it difficult to reach a consensus within their own union, let alone when there are three or four unions operating in the same territory with a duplication of effort.
I am not against the idea of a national farm union for specific purposes, the same kind of purpose for which I am willing to support certain aspects of Bill C-197; that is, for the orderly marketing of agricultural products of all kinds throughout the Dominion of Canada and for export trade and interprovincial trade. I think we probably need a national farm union representing as many farmers in Canada as are willing to turn out and take an interest in their own affairs, and I would be willing to back such a movement in principle. I am merely outlining some of the difficulties we will face unless we see very clearly what we are about to do.
In Alberta we have at the present time a move toward union. We have Unifarm, which combines the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and what was previously known as the Farm Union of Alberta, both pursuing identical goals. They have now united under one leadership called Unifarm. At most of the farm meetings I have attended I have noticed this difficulty about consensus-the difficulty of interpretation of whom the farmer is, what type of people we are trying to support, and so forth.
There is a great difference between a man starting up on a homestead with no assets whatsoever in the way of sophisticated machinery and very little working capital, and a well organized farmer with a herd of 50 dairy cattle, 1,000 acres of wheat or 300 or 400 head of cattle. Who is to say that Canada Packers is not a farm if they should buy a feedlot and fatten cattle, or if they should go into the vertical integration of raising hogs and so have control of the hog raising industry all the way from the feedlot through the packing industry into the Safeway stores, where they are joint owners of the means of distribution.
I do not underestimate the difficulties that farmers face in trying to unionize in an efficient manner. Their difficulty is not only to get a consensus in Parliament but also within their own unions. The debates within the unions are long and heated. Although their objects are identical from the point of view of the outsider, the subtle differences which

divide them are difficult to iron out. I assume that in the end the ideal would be one strong farm union from one end of Canada to the other, whether or not the name suggested in this legislation is used, which would represent all types of farming in all phases of agriculture.
We all know, however, that in any consensus there will be a pressure group within the union itself. Any farm union, whether it be Unifarm or the one we are asking for in this legislation, has to decide whom it represents. Then the farmer gets into the same trouble as a labourer when he decides whether to join a trade union. The advantages of the closed shop are many, but in return he sacrifices his sovereignty and has very little bargaining power as an individual.
Within the farm union movement itself there is a contradiction. It is democratic in so far as you take a vote and expect everybody to go along with the consensus, but you run into difficulty.

subtopic: FARM PRODUCTS MARKETING AGENCIES BILL

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Olson that Bill C-197, to establish the National Farm Products Marketing Council and to authorize the establishment of national marketing agencies for farm products, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

subtopic: FARM PRODUCTS MARKETING AGENCIES BILL
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL MARKETING COUNCIL AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was previously convinced that Bill C-197 is a bad bill and I just want to say that after listening to the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) and the various arguments advanced on either side, as well as experiencing the attitude of the government in respect of the functioning of this House, I am even more convinced that we do not want this bill.
Certainly we cannot trust such power as this bill assumes for the government and an agency to be appointed by it, if democracy is to have any meaning at all to the people of Canada. This bill indicates quite clearly that the degree of power the government is seeking, as it relates to a government-appointed agency without necessary reference to the producers and the primary industry of agriculture or their organizations or the provincial governments, is far in excess of that which the agricultural industry and their representatives proposed. It could usurp completely the control that now rests in the hands of the primary producers and the provincial governments.
I have said that the drive to centralize primary production and to centralize the controls over primary production in respect of agriculture is not the result of inevitable trends but is the result of a conscious effort to create a completely centrally-placed society. Call it what you will, this is a tragedy for the agricultural industry and for the farmers of Canada, because I believe genuine farmers the world over throughout history have been noted for their sturdy independence. Surely this is a characteristic of the Canadian farmer.
As a section of society, farmers have always manifested the highest principles of citizenship. When heavy taxation played its deadly role in helping to destroy the 22375-7
independence of the Roman peasantry, one of the great positive influences in the Roman Empire was eroded. The peasant farmers destroyed the plans of the totalitarians. Even the Soviets, as they planned their economy under Stalin, were forced to liquidate millions of kulaks who refused to co-operate with their totalitarian style or plan.
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is a tragedy that in the name of efficiency and on the excuse that the farmers need help this type of legislation should be proposed. I suggest that the basic question which the basic producer must ask himself is this: If a farmer was economic ten years ago and if he has substantially increased his production in this period, why is he now said to be uneconomic? The answer, of course, is not simply that in some cases the prices of his products have fallen but that his financial costs have increased. The progressive increases in costs have offset the increased production and the tremendous efficiency which the agricultural industry in Canada has achieved.
Now, if all the costs are increasing-and no less an authority than the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) has said so-we are in serious trouble in Canada. We are in even more serious trouble because of the control over planning, production and distribution which is to lie authorized by Bill C-197, regardless of the platitudinous arguments we have heard contrarywise. The statute itself is very clear. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the argument that we are growing too much wheat, and that too many people are engaged in farming, is a fallacy. The problem the Canadian farmer has is that he must face the competition of the European economic community-from the Argentine where the cost of production is less, from the heavily subsidized agricultural industry in the United States and from the low-cost production of that agricultural country, Australia.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
The farmer is in difficulty. Farmers in the Common Market countries have problems; we recognize that. But in spite of a reduction in the number of farmers, the main problem there is still huge surpluses. Common Market agricultural regulations require that food be destroyed to keep prices stable. Is this what we want here? Is this what has been discussed at the meeting held in Ottawa this week? Common Market agricultural regulations also provide for subsidization of their farmers. If these subsidies can be paid to

The expert planners use the situation to keep advocating a still further reduction in the number of farmers in production, and that is the only information we have out of the meeting that was held here this week. I wish to come back to the simple point that the farmers of Canada are in a very serious predicament, and they will not be brought out of this by this kind of legislation. They will just be moved further into the morass.
The president of the Alberta wheat pool said a few days ago:
The relative position which Canadian farmers occupy in the world economic struggle has depreciated in the past year and in the past decade.
That is almost the understatement of the year because the economic struggle facing the Canadian farmer is not just on the world scene but is right here at home. It is almost inevitable that Canada must decide soon whether or not this country is going to maintain a viable agricultural industry. I maintain that it is not the bureaucrats, who will have the power under this legislation to completely control production, who have the answers.
