This is the most dangerous bill that we have ever had in this House in relation to the agricultural industry, and yet it is excused with platitu-tudes as being something that the farm organizations have asked for themselves. They asked for help, but they did not ask for this kind of legislation.
If we establish a National Farm Products Marketing Council which will authorize the government to set up national marketing agencies for any or all farm products without consultation with the farmers, without requiring consultation with the farm organizations 

or the provincial departments of agriculture, which way will we be heading? This bill goes far in excess of that proposed by representatives of the agricultural industry. It could completely usurp the authority which is now vested in the hands of the primary producers and the provincial departments of agriculture.
In summary, we on this side of the House are opposing this bill for some very real reasons. With the exception of western wheat and fluid milk, the cabinet will be able to place any farm product under a national marketing agency without reference to Parliament, to provincial governments or even to the farmers themselves. I can hear the Minister of Agriculture saying, "Oh, yes; it says in the bill that first there must be a public hearing". But what does a public hearing do in the way of a check or a control, or in representing the opinion of the farmers or ensuring their participation?
Such an agency would have the power to determine the quantity, price, time and place at which any product or any variety, class or grade of product would be marketed in domestic or export trade. The agency could require farmers to obtain licences to grow, produce or market agricultural commodities. I do not like to refer to agricultural policies that are used by certain countries in eastern Europe, but this is so similar to those policies that it causes one to shudder. Furthermore, these same countries today are discovering that they cannot reach their maximum production under that kind of policy. They have had to go back to encouraging the individual to supplement his production on his little plot of land.
Such a marketing agency would have the power to collect charges to cover the cost of the marketing agency's operations, determining what the farmer would get in an initial, interim or final payment. Grain farmers this year know that these charges eliminated their final payment altogether. The bill states that inspectors could be appointed with broad powers to search for regulated commodities and to examine the farmers' books and documents-yes, and even put farmers in jail if it is thought they do not co-operate as they should. It could assume the responsibility for farm operations from production through selling, pricing, packaging, transportation and storage.
I do not believe the federal government should have the power which this bill would give them to appoint the various agencies that they may think are necessary, because it

gives them power for complete decision-making in the agricultural industry and it could reduce that industry to nothing more than a public utility. So I appeal to all members of the House, to the farmers and to all those who know agriculture to recognize this bill for what it is, because I am convinced it is a bad bill.

As I travelled across Canada I was struck by how much western Canada needs leadership in this field, yet we in Canada have two ministries, two vast departments supposedly trying to help the farmer market his products.

If you will bear with me for a moment, I would like to read part of a poem from "The Tales of the Pioneer" written by that well-known pioneer of Alberta, Ferg James. This is what he said about the cross-eyed rooster. We have two ministers, and the farmers are wondering at which of them they are looking. They are like a hen in the barnyard, wondering which minister and which piece of legislation will really help them.
The Minister without Portfolio in charge of the Wheat Board brought down a piece of legislation called operation LIFT which was very well received by the farmers. Some people called it WARP, others called it LIFT which means Lower Income For Tomorrow, and the common opinion in western Canada is that it is FLOP. As the debate has continued and I have had an opportunity to study the bill and to refer to what has been said by members on this side of the House, I have reached the conclusion that Bill C-197 in its present form is one of the most ingenious pieces of political deception ever to have been foisted on our unsuspecting agricultural industry.
Mr. Speaker, if this bill is enacted in its present form, it will make the so-called "great leap forward"-the Russian five-year plan, which turned out to be the great leap backward-look like the proverbial Sunday school picnic. The Minister of Agriculture

May 7, 1970
(Mr. Olson) who is sponsoring this legislation might just as well resign right now, or he will be forced to do so at a later date unless he takes steps at once to change the whole principle underlying this bill. In other words, if he accepts the principle outlined in the amendment just put forward by my hon. friend from Crowfoot, there may be some hope for the minister's survival; otherwise I suspect he will suffer dire consequences.
It is true that farmers and farm organizations have had considerable experience in production control and the operation of marketing agencies within provincial boundaries. These experiments have met with varying degrees of success. It is agreed that agriculture should come within the general sphere of federal agencies in cases where this is necessary and practicable, but only under a system which ensures that the farmer will have the final say in his own destiny by exercising control over decisions related both to production and to marketing. In a free democratic society, this is no more than justice and, basically speaking, it is the principle adhered to in other segments of our economy. The bill pretends to have this result, but in fact the very opposite would happen if it were passed in its present form.
It is interesting to note that the minister and the government seem awfully anxious to get this legislation into the House, have it given second reading without too much discussion and then push it into committee just as Parliament is about to recess for the summer, using the old propaganda device that it must be passed quickly because it is so important to agriculture and that if it is held up, the opposition is to blame. Well, the tactic will not work this time, because some very responsible people and organizations have already called a halt in connection with this iniquitous bill and want to see where we are going. Ministers of agriculture in several provinces have taken this stand, and only two weeks ago a telegram was directed to the Minister of Agriculture by members of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange speaking for themselves and other agricultural businesses.
They said they were deeply concerned by the implications of Bill C-197 and did not believe that producers, consumers, trade groups or members of the House of Commons could give considered thought to it without having received the report of the agricultural task force as essential background material. The telegram went on to say:
We urgently request that final consideration of this bill be withheld until the House, the Standing

May 7. 1970	COMMONS
Committee on Agriculture and the public have been given an opportunity to study the task force report and all relevant proposals.
This is a reasonable suggestion. My advice to the minister and to members of the government is that they call a halt to this legislation on the basis of the advice they are getting, or at least accept the amendment put forward by my hon. friend from Crowfoot in order to remove the concern felt by a great many of those who have had a chance to consider the implications of this bill.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend several of the previous speakers in this debate on the stand they have taken with regard to this questionable legislation. I have already mentioned my hon. friend from Crowfoot. I wish also to mention the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), the hon. member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Danforth) and the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). In his speech the other night the latter referred to the bill before us as being the most dangerous, dictatorial, damaging and destructive piece of legislation ever brought in by a Minister of Agriculture. He described it as one which particularly attacks western agriculture. I sincerely agree with these statements. At the present time, western farmers are struggling for their very existence. They are faced with want in a land of plenty. Last month's labour review figures indicated that some 7,000 workers were forced to leave the province of Saskatchewan to look for work. What a terrible loss of human resources, Mr. Speaker, apart from the economic aspects of the situation.
A further blow to the small farmer was the government's recent application of the LIFT program, or what has commonly been referred to as the farmers' income reduction plan. Here again is an example of government legislation, ill-conceived, hastily prepared and hurriedly applied to an industry which did not know what was happening to it. Oh yes, the minister tells us he had the agreement of the industry, but it is passing strange that hardly a soul in western Canada wants to admit he had any part in operation LIFT whatsoever.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
In speaking to this bill, I want to warn farmers in all parts of Canada to study the bill in all its ramifications, to benefit from their sad experience with the present government by seeing to it that they personally and their farm organizations collectively call a halt to 22375-8
DEBATES	6721
Farm, Products Marketing Agencies Bill the quick implementation of this proposed legislation, at least in its present form; and to make sure that sufficient time be made available for them to appear before the Standing Committee on agriculture as well as to have a thorough debate on the important issues among their various farm groups.
Rather than continue in generalities, let us look at some of the specifics of this bill. A study of Bill C-197 indicates quite clearly that the degree of power sought by the government goes far in excess of that proposed by representatives of the agricultural industry, and could usurp completely the control now vested in the hands of primary producers and provincial governments. In its present form, this legislation grants to a council and marketing agency, whose total membership are government appointees, absolute power to establish agencies, to license and allocate quota production and to control pricing, processing, marketing, storing, distribution and packaging of any farm product or products by government decree without any reference to Parliament. Just think of that, Mr. Speaker! The bill goes on to provide for supply management or controlled production at the discretion of a government bureau whose power, as stated in the bill, goes so far as to "do all such other things as are necessary or incidental to the exercise of any of its powers or the carrying out of any of its functions under this act".
The House has just heard the discourse of the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) who emphasized and re-emphasized in better words than I could the worries and concerns of individual farmers and of agriculture in general. This government bureau can impose such licence fees, levies or charges on farmers as are necessary to finance the agency or agencies on a self-sustaining basis without appropriations from Parliament. In other words, I presume this board of bureaucrats will be appointed by the government and will completely dominate the farm industry segment it is set up to supervise; but the farmer will be called on to pay the whole shot, including the salaries involved. To go further into the offensive part of this legislation, the bill states that any person who violates any provisions of the act or regulations is either guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, or is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.
It is my opinion that under the powers granted under Bill C-197 the government
May 7, 1970
6722	COMMONS DEBATES
Farm Products Marketing Agencies Bill
could entrust to an appointed bureau the complete decision-making process in the entire agricultural and allied agri-industry of Canada, reducing it to the category of another public utility. Just think of this concept as applied to our normal life on a farm! Farming has always been a special way of life where those engaged in it lived, moved and had their being in a special environment where they were free to work, rest, play, commune with nature and make their own decisions without regimentation. The mould into which farmers would be forced should the present provisions in this bill be applied to them is the very antithesis of this state.
I am not an expert on the constitution, but I have some very grave doubts about some of the proposals in this bill, which I fear would run afoul of provincial jurisdictions. Some say the bill in its present form could contravene the Bill of Rights. It appears from reading the bill that under clause 2 the federal government is developing power to coerce the provinces. Let me quote from clause 2, subclause (e)(vi), which provides as follows:
(vi) the imposition and collection by the appropriate agency of levies or charges from persons engaged in the growing or production of the regulated product for, or in the marketing thereof in, interprovincial or export trade and for such purposes classifying those persons into groups and specifying the levies or charges, if any, proposed in respect of the members of each such group-
The bill goes on to state in clause 31, which deals with agreements:
With the approval of the Governor in Council, the minister may, on behalf of the government of Canada, enter into an agreement with any province providing for the performance by an agency on behalf of the province, of functions relating to intraprovincial trade in a regulated product or products in relation to which the agency may exercise its powers and for such other matters relating thereto as may be agreed upon by the Minister and the government of the province.
These provisions give the federal government the economic power, whether consciously or unconsciously employed, to coerce almost all existing provincial marketing boards to fall in line with federal structures or force unorganized producers in provinces to establish marketing boards subservient to federal criteria. Since the plan can be established for a group, a national agency could be established without the unanimous or even majority support of the provinces. Further, this plan could destroy the extraprovincial market or invade the provincial market of a renegade sector of the industry. I think my colleague for Crowfoot emphasized that par-
ticular point. Unorganized or independent sectors would be forced to comply; they could not resist an effective federal supply management plan.
Here it seems that constitutionally the federal government could arrange with a particular province delegations of powers that are clearly detrimental to other provinces, without the consent of those other provinces. Where does this leave the often referred to principles of the Fulton-Favreau formula? I could go on at greater length, but I think I have made my point as to why I have grave doubts about this legislation in its present state.
In conclusion, I would like to refer to the fact that the National Farmers Union, who have often been referred to as leaning too far to the left, are greatly concerned about this bill and its implications. It is also interesting to note that in the April issue of "The Canada Poultryman" my friend, the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Pringle), a member of the government benches who has had considerable experience in marketing boards, is quoted as saying:
It was my hope that some positive recognition would be given to the fact that the act is intended to provide a means for proper production planning and marketing of primary products in the first instance and would therefore stipulate a majority of producers should be charged with the responsibility of administering the act by election to the governing council.
The hon. member I have just quoted went on to say in the article that he was also disturbed about clause 13 of the bill. This warning, coming from a member of the government ranks, should indicate that the official opposition is on the right track when we advocate that a very serious look be taken at this questionable piece of legislation.

subtopic: FARM PRODUCTS MARKETING AGENCIES BILL
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL MARKETING COUNCIL AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in this debate on Bill C-197 which many had thought would be the Magna Carta for agriculture and for the marketing of agricultural products for which the industry had been waiting for many long, frustrated years. We on this side of the House were concerned at the introduction of the bill at this time when the task force had not brought in firm recommendations. We wonder about the minister proceeding at this point with such a massive proposal, one that affects every facet of Canadian agriculture.
The principle of the bill, which is that of orderly marketing, finds favour on both sides of the House. Only when you read the clauses
May 7, 1970	COMMONS
of the bill do you begin to realize that instead of being the Magna Carta for agriculture the bill will be, if passed in its present form, a sentence of state control over agriculture of a sort seldom, if ever, seen in a free, democratic country. It is for that reason that we on this side of the House feel compelled to rise in our places and give the views of those who will be affected by the provisions of the bill.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
The people who will be affected are not just those engaged in farming or in growing the product. They will include everyone who is in any way affected by a farm product from the seed to the sale. It is only necessary to look at the bill very quickly, as some members have done here today, in order to understand the reason we take such strong objection to it. We do not mind some form of supply management or supply marketing. We do not mind having orderly direction given to some of the chaotic marketing practices in this country, but we absolutely oppose the power which the government is delegating to the cabinet. The phrase used in the bill is "the Governor in Council". We all know what that means: it means the cabinet. We absolutely oppose a measure in which the government would be delegating to the cabinet the rights, responsibilities and challenges in respect of agriculture, with no producer participation. That is the fundamental flaw in this bid.
If anyone challenges my comment in respect of cabinet control, all he need do is quickly read some of the clauses in the bill. Clause 3 is the clause setting up the council. It says that there shall be not less than three and not more than nine members appointed by the Governor in Council, as the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) has said. It goes on to say that those three or nine members may not appoint the chairman or vice-chairman. I shall not quibble about that. The interesting thing is that in subclause (4) of clause 3 it states that if anyone is absent, the cabinet can appoint a substitute to take over. That perhaps is not too important either. Basically, however, it is the cabinet that appoints the council. Then we come to the agencies the council will set up. This is set out in clause 19. Again there is a complete vacuum in respect of the word "producer". In clause 19 it is the Governor in Council that appoints the members of the agency. Again it sets out that the agencies and the chairman shall be appointed by the cabinet and that the vice-chairman shall be appointed by the cabinet.

Farm Products Marketing Agencies Bill
If for any reason a member of an agency cannot attend a meeting, the cabinet can appoint a replacement, I suppose on a temporary basis. I hope at some time the minister will explain subclause (4) of clause 19. This is the subclause which concerns the setting up of this temporarily appointed member. This is the first occasion on which I have seen such a provision in a bill. This could have serious implications, I suppose, if we were to consider an extreme example-and I suppose this bill is extreme. The minister could say to his colleagues, "Let us make sure that some of these people are absent so that we can slip in some substitutes in order to pass the order of the day". I hope the minister will explain the necessity for this clause. Basically, it is the cabinet which appoints the council and the agencies to deal with the farm products. In clause 18 it is also the cabinet which decides what farm product is to be proclaimed.
So the words "participatory democracy" ring very hollow indeed when we consider this bill which affects the bread and butter not only of the farmers of this land but all Canadians who eat the produce of the farm. Producer participation is completely absent here. The minister seems to take great pleasure in saying that there is producer participation. This afternoon at one time in the debate he pointed out in respect of clause 8 that there will be a public hearing and that this is producer participation. Good gracious, there are many ways in which to have public hearings in this country. Many Canadians today are affected by the CPR and CNR rail line abandonments and the CPR and CNR passenger service discontinuance. They have public hearings. I should like to see a member or the minister appear before the Canadian Transport Commission and fight the power and prestige of the CNR or the CPR in an effort to prevent rail line discontinuance or passenger service discontinuance. I do not think they would be very successful, but there is a public hearing.
We had the CRTC public hearings at the Skyline Hotel a couple of weeks ago in respect of that commission's proposals concerning Canadian content. The organized broadcasting industry could present its proposals and alternatives, but the average citizen would have found it pretty difficult to make any real point. There have been hearings in one form or another in respect of the white paper. However, the best test of the laws of efficacy and efficiency as well as con-
May 7, 1970
6724	COMMONS DEBATES
Farm Products Marketing Agencies Bill structive proposals in respect of public hearings is the committees system of this House. I dare the minister to stand up some time during this debate and tell us how many committee reports of this House have been implemented by the government, even those which have had the unanimous consent or practically the unanimous consent of all members regardless of party line. But, Mr. Speaker, a committee meeting is in effect a public hearing.
Perhaps by the end of this session, and certainly by the end of this Parliament, the role of committees will have to be defined so that the people who wish to present briefs will finally know whether there is any purpose in appearing before committees, and so that members will know whether or not it is a waste of time to spend hours and hours listening to witnesses, briefs, proposals and recommendations which are then shunted aside by the government. I do not blame the government completely, because there is a fundamental flaw in our system. When you have cabinet responsibility you cannot have committee responsibility. I do not know of a single example so far of a committee recommendation which has superseded a government proposal. It seems to me at first blush that this fundamental flaw in respect of the cabinet and the responsibility which flows therefrom under the parliamentary system should have been faced up to at the time of the stimulation engendered in respect of the just society during the election campaign of 1968. We should start to define the policies which governments should follow.
I digressed, Mr. Speaker, because members of this House are sick to the teeth with public hearings and with having 14 committee meetings meeting on each Tuesday and Thursday. These are great public hearings at which information flows back and forth. But what comes from them? Members become frustrated and depressed about having put in time on these committees. But these are public hearings. The minister this afternoon suggested that perhaps this would be a way in which the producers could participate. Of course they can participate with their tongues and their ears, but can they participate in the decisions? There is not a single comma, clause or anything in this bill that would indicate that the producer is to be given any voice of his own. Of course, the minister may point out that some of the members of the council can be representatives of producer groups. I do not think he will appoint all public service 
or fishermen from Newfoundland to deal with wheat in the west. But that is not producer participation in decisions concerning the producers who have had representative groups participating and mingling with the appointees of the minister.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
This thesis makes a sham and a mockery of the word "participation" and the words "producer participation". In fact, clause 8 does not contain one word about producers, and a quick look at the bill tonight-which I read in great detail many days ago before coming into the House-shows that the word "producer" does not appear anywhere in the bill other than in clause 6 (2)(b), which is a most interesting clause. It reads as follows:
In carrying out its duties the council shall (b) have regard to the interests of consumers of farm products-
Then mention is made of those engaged in the marketing of the products and only in the third place are the interests of producers of farm products mentioned. This is the only time that producers are mentioned in this bill. First priority is given to consumers and then to distributors.
How can a bill that is supposed to be the Magna Carta and the new broom to help the marketing of farm products represent fairly and justly the interests of the agricultural industry when in the same clause the interests of consumers and distributors are mentioned? If the bill is to mean anything, this fundamental flaw in clause 6 (2)(b) should be corrected.
It is inevitable, and it is the law of life and an admission of reality, that the consumer wants to get his goods at the cheapest price while the producer wants to sell his goods for the highest price. How is the council in all its wisdom-even though there is not one producer group represented, as set out in the bill in any formal way-to balance off the interests of these two fundamentally opposed groups? I as a consumer want to buy my bread, milk cheese and potatoes for peanuts, if I can. On the other hand, the farmer wants to buy his machinery for peanuts, if he can. Yet in Bill C-197, clause 6 (2Kb), these fundamentally irreconcilable interests are balanced. I do not see how the minister or the council can pretend that anything will come of this in the interests of the producers, if this clause means what it says. Yet this is the only place in the bill where producers are mentioned.
May 7, 1970	COMMONS
This bill, if not amended, will give absolute control to the cabinet over any agricultural product from seed to sale. All of us in this House, even those across the way who think farmers putting the seed in the land will be the only ones affected by this bill, had better take another look at it because it will affect a product from its planting through its growth right down to its distribution and marketing. The control goes so far as to allow the cabinet, without producer participation, to give licences to those who shall participate in the whole operation and grow the produce. If you get the licence to grow the product, you are then faced with a quota limiting how much you can grow and ultimately how much you get for it.
There may be a case in some Socialist or state-controlled societies for giving this type of control to the cabinet or to Parliament. I doubt if there is, but at least in Parliament the people affected have a voice and their viewpoints can be expressed. There can then be a cross-examination on the policies put forward. But if this act goes through unamended, the council, through the cabinet and the cabinet appointees, will have complete control over agricultural products from seed to sale, complete control over beef, hogs or whales-if whales were an agricultural product-with no say being given to elected members and no say being given to the producers who grow the goods.
We on this side are in favour of co-ordination, but we are not in favour of complete cabinet control. We on this side are in favour of direction in agricultural policies, but we are not in favour of a dictatorship over agricultural policies. We on this side are in favour of regulations and of a regulated agricultural industry, but we oppose and will oppose to our last breath regimentation of that industry.
If the government wishes to control farm products tonight, how do we know that tomorrow they will not want to do the same with primary products? Is that the intent of the minister and his government? Will they be moving into lumber now? They are partly into fish marketing, since they require quotas and licences for boats. I could go into that subject at length. Once the government moves into the primary industries it will want to move into the manufacturing industries and establish licences to control who can manufacture what and how much.
That is the thesis and principle behind the bill as presently drafted and proposed by the
DEBATES	6725
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion minister. Once the government moves into the manufacturing industry, what will stop them from controlling the professions and starting to give out licences? They will not let the Bar Society or the Medical Society administer their own groups. There might be good reason for making some changes there, but is the minister supporting this thesis and principle? I know there are some in this House who want such changes. I hope the minister will join his true friends to my left. I for one am absolutely opposed to a bill that gives the cabinet complete control over the agricultural industry and thereby logically suggests an extension of its power.
My time is almost up. I say that if this bill goes through, then the just society will fast become a controlled society. Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock?

THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-EFFECT ON EMPLOYMENT OF ANTI-INFLATION POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 27 I asked the following question of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen):
In view of the fact that the March unemployment statistics have revealed that nearly 40 per cent of the unemployed in Canada are under the age of 25, can the minister indicate to the House whether his department has begun any new youth programs that might help alleviate this situation?
The minister, after I asked him whether or not he could make a statement on Motions, said that he would not. It appears to me that the minister did not really consider this problem to be very severe. For that reason I will spend four or five minutes tonight trying to outline some of the reasons why I think the government, the Department of Manpower and Immigration and the minister must give this new problem top priority.
First of all, 40 per cent of the unemployed of Canada are under the age of 25. This does not include university students who are coming out of universities now, nor does it include technical school students or even some of the high school students coming out of school in June. Here I am talking about the regular people who are on the labour market all year round. Many are unskilled. Many
6726	COMMONS DEBATES	May 7, 1970
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion need new training. They need new outlets to be opened for them. Others have skills but because of the government's policies on inflation they find themselves out of work. Some are even university graduates. For example, teachers in Saskatchewan and in other provinces cannot find work because of the general economic picture throughout the country.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
I have only a few minutes tonight, and in order to emphasize the point, Mr. Speaker, I wish briefly to try to put you in the shoes of one of these young people who may be unemployed. This man may have a family. He may be married and have two or three children. He may not have a particular skill. For one reason or another he may have dropped out of school in the hope that society would offer him something, that society had a role for him to play. Society does promise young people great things through magazines, newspapers and television. We raise the expectations of young people. We say we are offering them a chance, an alternative in Canada. But when these young people get out in the world, in many instances the door is slammed in their face. As a result, 40 per cent of the unemployed in Canada today are under the age of 25 years.
The whole picture of youth unemployment means many things. First of all it means that there will be more frustration in our young society. There will be an alienation from the government, from the country and the society in which we live. Unemployment places many young people in the vicious circle of poverty. That means many things psychologically and sociologically. It means that many of these young people will drop out of society and into some of the youth cults that we have today in all big cities. It creates unrest and the whole phenomenon of protest.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we have some members getting up in this House and asking why is there protest, and why are demonstrations going on in Canada and in the United States? In some of these demonstrations at times there is violence because the young people are frustrated, because they do not know where they are going or what opportunities they have. I do not condone violence; I do not think any of us do. But I try to understand why violence occurs, why these young people are unhappy, why they are looking for something, and what alternatives they want. I think this is very important. I think society, Canada and the government must really con-
[Mr. Nystrom.l
sider why many young people are alienated from society. The fact that 40 per cent of our unemployed are under age 25 is one very good reason why there is a lot of frustration and alienation in the youth community.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), when justifying his policies, said that unemployment is just one of the unfortunate consequences of the fight against inflation. Are these young people, who just happen to be unemployed, the unfortunate consequences that the Prime Minister talked about? Are we going to put these young people in positions where they do not have chances and opportunities? I suggest we should not, because if we do we are not only destroying their lives but we are adding new problems to those we already have in our society and in Canada. This is something that is highly unfair. For this reason I think the minister should make a statement on what plans members of the government have to tackle this problem. What retraining are they offering these young people? What general types of plans do they have? It is time we stopped ignoring this problem and stopped treating these young people with contempt.
I know that many people on both sides of this House look at young people in the way that President Nixon and Vice-President Spiro Agnew do. Recently the U.S. Vice-President said that these people causing trouble on campuses are just a bunch of bums. That is one of the reasons why President Nixon's youth adviser resigned today. He said he was resigning because the President does not want to try to understand young people. Let us avoid falling into that trap in Canada. We can avoid this if we reorient our policies and set out priorities for government, and in turn for our whole society.
With that I plead with the Parliamentary Secretary who is answering tonight on behalf of the minister: I ask that he have a real good talk with the minister, who is not here tonight, and try to emphasize the importance of this problem which could become very acute.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in replying to the hon. member we say that we share his concern for the youth of this country who are unemployed, and I am sure that the minister and the Department of Manpower and Immigration also are deeply concerned with this problem. The problems of today's disadvantaged or unemployed youth are vastly more complex than the mere fact
May 7, 1970	COMMONS
of being without a job. The manpower counsellors in the Canada Manpower centres, who are available to all Canadian youth who wish to seek their help, know that the problems of young people are complex. The dimension of the problems in this sector of the labour force has warranted the establishment of special programs to assist young people entering the labour force.
Over and above the services normally provided to students through counsellors working in Canada Manpower centres at 55 universities or other post-secondary institutions the department also plays an important role in providing consultative services to other government departments and outside agencies, to vocational counsellors in school and in providing labour market information and career information to young people.
The hon. member spoke of the unemployed who are under 25 years of age. I should say that the average age of persons referred to training under the Canada Manpower training program is slightly more than 26 years. By inference, this means that a large number of persons under 25 years of age are in training, preparing themselves to find and hold jobs or undertake better jobs than they had before receiving training. For example, 8| per cent of the approximately 300,000 persons referred to training in 1968-69 were 19 years of age or under. That means about 25,000 teenagers were helped by the Canada Manpower training program. Another 34.7 per cent, or 103,000 trainees, were in the 20 to 24 years of age bracket.
One of the pilot projects undertaken by the department is the youth employment service in Toronto, for which the department provides a counselling capability. Under the YES project, which was undertaken in co-operation with the Toronto Rotary Club, disadvantaged youth are interviewed and counselled to take their place on the labour market. A similar pilot project is under way in Montreal. As the department learns more about these attempts at reaching out to the youth of the country, better organized programs can be considered within the department's resources.

Has the Department of National Defence requested or put into effect a change in the route or direction of Strategic Air Command B-52 flights over Saskatchewan and Alberta as a result of many protests, particularly those by flying clubs in Saskatchewan and Alberta?

Prior to the announcement of these training flights the Minister of National Defence courteously informed me, along with a number of other members, that these flights were about to commence and that part of the route would be over our constituencies. In explaining some of the details he stated that no weapon would be carried on the aircraft. Dealing with the low-level portion of the route he also said:
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
The low-level portion of the route is located over sparsely populated areas at an altitude of 1,000 to 2,000 feet above the ground depending on local terrain. The Department of Transport has reviewed the proposed route and agrees with it from the technical and operational view-point. Utilization of the route will be on the continuous basis from April 2, 1970 to September 23, 1970.
Later, in the press release that was issued by the Department of National Defence, the description of the low-level route varied somewhat from that described in the minister's letter. The press release said that the aircraft will enter Canada south of Weyburn, Saskatchewan, at a high altitude and start

descending north of Prince Albert to a height varying from 800 to 1,000 feet above the ground.
I wrote to the Minister of National Defence protesting these flights. I said:
At this time X wish to make known to you my unhappiness and disagreement with the policy involved in this announcement. I would presume that these arrangements have been made under the auspices ol NORAD. You will be familiar, of course, with the opposition of the New Democratic Party to the present NORAD arrangement. Furthermore, my understanding is that Canada has no control over the disposition of the pilots after they have completed their training. Presumably some of the pilots will be despatched to Viet Nam to take part in the conflict there. I am opposed to any association on the part of Canada in situations which contribute to the continuation or prolongation of the Viet Nam conflict or the participation of the United States in that war.
I believe I should draw to your attention that you can expect very valid complaints from many people that these training flights as indicated on the map supplied to me, will direct planes to fly over the city of Regina which, in my view, is completely unnecessary.
The minister answered in a letter dated March 20, explaining that with respect to aircraft flying at a level of between 800 and 1,000 feet above ground level the perceived noise level of a B-52 overhead is 30 to 40 decibels, with the level increasing to 100 decibels when the aircraft is 60 degrees past the observer. The minister went on to make comparisons, saying that the noise level of a heavy truck at highway speeds is 100 decibels as it passes an observer at a distance of 50 feet. Similar observations are made with respect to jackhammers and other such objects.
Later there was a protest from the Shell-brook-Leask Flying Club about these flights. They said that they interfered with their operations. They noted in the first place that low altitudes are proposed over populated areas and said as follows:
The low-level flying extends from Clarke Lake north to Marcelin-Blaine Lake and proceeds westerly passing just south of North Battleford and then into Alberta. The proposed altitude is calculated to be between 800-1,800 feet above ground level.
This crosses two VFR student-training flight routes between Prince Albert, North Battleford, and Saskatoon for solo cross-country.
This crosses several private landing strips-
This crosses populated areas ... Debden, Mont Nebo, Leask, Marcelin, Blaine lake, Krydor, Haf-ford-
They say that to the best of their knowledge air-to-air communication between military and general aviation aircraft is impossible due to differences in radio frequencies. [Mr. Burton.}
There is an erratic scheduling of sorties and there is interference with their entire summer flying schedule of light aircraft.
I urge the government to take the necessary steps to discontinue these training flights, in the first place because they involve training for military purposes of foreign military personnel over Canadian soil. It is a type of military training that is completely unnecessary, and it takes place over Canadian soil. It also involves us in a further step in terms of our implied involvement in the Viet Nam conflict.
Second, I suggest that the high altitude flights over Regina at between 30,000 and 35,000 feet can interfere with Air Canada and other long-distance flights which overfly the city of Regina. Third, as I have already indicated, they constitute a distinct interference with the operations of light aircraft and the low-level operations of the flying routes which extend from somewhere near the Prince Albert National Park south to near Saskatoon, west to North Battleford, and west-southwest in the province of Alberta before the end of the low-level portion of the route is completed. Thus, I urge the government to reconsider its stand on this matter and see that these flights are discontinued at once.

Mr. Speaker, to begin with I find myself at a slight disadvantage because I could not possibly guess from the question asked by the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Burton) on April 21 what the exact subject of his complaint would be tonight. I am therefore somewhat ill-prepared to answer the questions he has put. I will be getting in touch with him at a later date to allay some of his fears, particularly his fear that these training flights are in any way connected with the involvement of the United States in Viet Nam: the type of training given, as I understand it, is of a completely different technique.
I can, however, give some reply which may reassure him on one point. To the best of my knowledge the Department of National Defence has received only one complaint from a flying club-this was from the Shell-brook Flying Club in Saskatchewan. As a result of this complaint the Department of Transport issued further and more detailed explanatory instructions on the way in which private pilots' associations could obtain detailed knowledge of flight timings. I am told
May 7, 1970	COMMONS
that an official of the Shellbrook Flying Club expressed satisfaction with these arrangements.
There is a little to add on this subject. I should like to emphasize that these SAC training flights were only approved after arrangements had been worked out with the governments of both Saskatchewan and Alberta. As hon. members know, flying is carried out on Mondays to Fridays. All commercial airlines and private pilots have received notification from the Department of Transport of the training route. I hope this reply is satisfactory. As I say, I shall be in touch with the hon. member later as to points I have not covered in the short time at my disposal.

Mr. Speaker, on April 27 I directed a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) with regard to the use in agriculture of the chemical 2-4-5T. I did so because the dangers inherent in the use of this chemical are very serious. The minister in his reply said:
It may be we will further restrict the use of 2-4-5T. I would draw to the hon. member's attention, however, that there has been no residue of this chemical found in any food and, indeed, if there should be, the Food and Drug Directorate would withhold that food. In other words, there is a nil tolerance.
I take the expression "nil tolerance" to mean that the human body cannot tolerate any fraction of this particular chemical. The minister was saying that if there should be any residue of this chemical found in food, the Food and Drug Directorate would withhold it because human beings cannot tolerate this particular chemical. DDT has a lifetime residual effect of 15 years; it can persist in natural surroundings such as foliage for that long. Do we intend to wait until the effects of this chemical show up in some of our food and then, because there is a nil tolerance, have that food destroyed as unfit for human consumption? Are we going to wait until we are where we are now, with the fishermen standing unemployed at some of our important lakes and rivers? Are we going to wait around until eventually we find our farmers in the same position? There is an even more disastrous effect. I should like to refer to a CBC news report broadcast on May 5 as follows:
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
The United States Department of Agriculture yesterday announced that the herbicide 2-4-5T has been banned for certain uses because of its potential to cause birth defects in humans.

According to another news broadcast on the CBC on May 4, when this defoliant was used in Viet Nam, no doubt with scant notice to recommended rates of application, birth abnormalities did appear and this resulted in the banning of the chemical in the U.S. as well as by the military in Viet Nam. Yet we still permit this chemical to be used in certain areas, on lawns and around homes, despite the fact we know it is dangerous. If there was no other chemical that could be used for this purpose, the situation would be bad enough. But in all likelihood other chemicals could be found to do a similar job, and to do it effectively.
Therefore, I fail to see any justification for the continuing use of this chemical. For what moral or logical reason do we permit the chemical to be used, in view of the fact that the Food and Drug Directorate has advised the Department of Agriculture that it is dangerous to human life and health and, perhaps even worse than that, dangerous to unborn children? Think how horrible it would be for a mother who nurses a child that is bom with deformities caused by the use of such a chemical.
In a report by Peter Calami of Southam News Services dealing with experiments on rats, it is stated that use of this chemical made the rats look "doggish". The report states that rats born with malformations looked more like pups than rats. That statement is attributed to Dr. Alec Morrison, deputy directer general of the Food and Drug Directorate. According to the same report, about 43,000 acres in western Canada were sprayed with the herbicide last year, mostly to control hemp nettles in wheat, oats and barley. I suggest that with a minimum of effort the Department of Agriculture could find other chemicals that would do this job. I submit the department should not license chemical companies, which I will not name in my speech because I do not want to single out certain companies, to continue to manufacture and to distribute this very dangerous chemical.
This is the reason I have taken time tonight on the late show. I wanted to bring some of these facts to light in the hope of persuading the Department of Agriculture to take the action they should take to protect human health and well-being in Canada.
